notes.meaning: Aaron's two oldest sons took their incense pans, put coals in them, and burned incense with regular fire instead of fire from the holy altar. God had not commanded them to do this, and they acted without His direction. Their careless pride led them to treat God's sacred rules as something they could change.

differ.view: This passage establishes that God may only be worshiped in ways He has explicitly commanded in Scripture, and human inventions in worship are forbidden.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Some traditional interpreters discussed whether the priests committed a mortal sin or a lesser fault that was fully paid for by their sudden physical death.

notes.meaning: A blast of fire came out from the Lord's presence and struck Nadab and Abihu dead right where they stood. The fire acted like lightning, killing them instantly without burning their bodies or scorching their clothes. This severe judgment showed the whole camp that God's holiness must never be treated lightly.

Moses reminded Aaron that God had declared He will show His holiness through those who come near Him to serve, and His honor must be seen by all the people. When Aaron heard this, he stayed completely silent and did not complain against God. Even through his crushing grief, Aaron accepted that the Lord's judgment was just.

Moses summoned Mishael and Elzaphan, cousins of Aaron, and told them to carry the dead bodies away from the sanctuary and outside the camp. The cousins obeyed and carried the two men by their priestly tunics. God did not allow Aaron or his surviving priest sons to touch the corpses, because that would have made them ceremonially unclean.

Moses ordered Aaron and his remaining sons not to practice ordinary mourning rituals, such as tearing their clothes or leaving their hair messy. If the priests showed outward grief, it might look like they were protesting God's righteous decision, which would bring judgment on the whole camp. The rest of the nation of Israel was permitted to mourn the terrible loss caused by God's fire.

The priests were warned not to leave the entrance of the Tent of Meeting to attend the funeral, or they would die. The holy anointing oil had set them apart for God's work, meaning their sacred duties came ahead of family ties. Aaron and his sons obeyed Moses and remained at their place of service.

The Lord spoke directly to Aaron, commanding that neither he nor his sons drink wine or beer when entering the Tent of Meeting. Disobeying this lasting rule would bring death. God wanted His ministers to have completely clear minds so they would never make reckless mistakes during worship.

differ.view: The placement of this command immediately after the deaths suggests that Nadab and Abihu had been drinking when they offered unauthorized fire.
Some scholars note there is no certain proof the two sons were drunk, viewing this statute simply as a general rule for sanctuary order.

notes.meaning: Remaining sober allowed the priests to clearly tell the difference between what was set apart for God and what was ordinary. They also had to decide what was pure and what was contaminated in daily religious life. A confused mind could lead to treating sacred things as common.

The priests were responsible for teaching the people of Israel every law the Lord had spoken through Moses. They could not guide the community faithfully if their thoughts were clouded by alcohol. Their sacred role included being teachers of the truth, not just workers at the altar.

Moses instructed Aaron and his surviving sons, Eleazar and Ithamar, to take the leftover grain offering and eat it without yeast near the altar. Because this food was most holy, it belonged only to the priests and had to be eaten within the sacred courtyard. Moses urged them to keep doing their duty even while carrying great sorrow.

The breast and thigh from the fellowship offerings were also given to Aaron's household as their ongoing share. Unlike the most holy grain offering, these parts could be eaten in any ceremonially clean place, and the priests' daughters were allowed to eat them too. God gave these gifts to care for the priest's whole family.

Moses searched carefully for the goat that had been offered for the people's sins and found that it had been completely burned up. He became angry with Eleazar and Ithamar for not eating the meat as the law required. Moses was eager to make sure every part of God's pattern was followed without mistake.

Moses asked why they had failed to eat the most holy sin offering in the court, since eating it was part of taking away the community's guilt. Atonement means repairing the broken relationship between God and sinners. Because the animal's blood had not been taken inside the Holy Place, the rules said the meat was to be eaten by the priests, not burned.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Scholars suggest that eating the purification offering removed magical ideas common in ancient religions, showing that cleansing came only from God's word rather than the ritual meat itself.

notes.meaning: Aaron answered Moses by pointing out that even after they had presented their sacrifices, this awful tragedy had struck his home. He asked whether eating the sacred sin offering with a weeping and broken heart would have truly pleased the Lord. Aaron did not act out of rebellion, but out of a reverent fear that his family's grief would spoil the holy meal.

When Moses heard Aaron's gentle explanation, he was completely satisfied. He saw that Aaron truly wanted to honor God rather than break His commands on purpose. God showed understanding and mercy to a grieving father who acted out of reverence.
